title: Myasthenic crisis after stopping medication: respiratory muscle (NMJ) failure
vignette: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to progressive weakness and dyspnea. The patient is visiting her niece, who says the patient forgot to bring her regular medications and has not been taking them for the past week. The patient began feeling weak and fatigued 3 days ago and has had shortness of breath since yesterday. Temperature is 37 C (98.6 F), blood pressure is 122/88 mm Hg, pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 24/min and shallow. On physical examination, the patient appears dyspneic with drooping at the eyelids and corners of the mouth. Her speech has a nasal quality. Arterial blood gas obtained on room air shows pH 7.32; PaCO2 is 52 mm Hg, PaO2 is 72 mm Hg, and HCO3 is 26 mEq/L. Bedside spirometry demonstrates decreased forced vital capacity. A pathologic process involving which of the following structures is the most likely cause of this patient's shortness of breath?

clues.text: has not been taking them for the past week
clues.note: Stopping myasthenia gravis medications (e.g., pyridostigmine) can precipitate a myasthenic crisis with worsening weakness and respiratory failure.

clues.text: drooping at the eyelids and corners of the mouth
clues.note: Ptosis and facial (bulbar) weakness are hallmark features of myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular junction disease).
Nasal, dysarthric speech reflects bulbar muscle weakness - characteristic of myasthenia gravis.
Hypercapnia (PaCO2 52 / normal ~40) with a low-normal pH signals HYPOVENTILATION from respiratory muscle weakness - impending respiratory failure.
Reduced forced vital capacity objectively demonstrates respiratory MUSCLE weakness (not airway/parenchymal disease).

whatMatters: Ptosis + bulbar (nasal) speech + rising CO2 + low forced vital capacity after stopping medication = MYASTHENIC CRISIS. Weakness of the RESPIRATORY MUSCLES (from neuromuscular junction failure) causes hypoventilation and hypercapnic respiratory failure. Answer B.
strategy: Localize the dyspnea: hypercapnia + low FVC + neuromuscular signs (ptosis, nasal speech) = respiratory MUSCLE (neuromuscular junction) failure, not a lung or airway problem. Reject brain-stem respiratory center (would spare voluntary breathing; no NMJ signs), pulmonary arteries (PE - no muscle weakness), and terminal airways/alveoli or upper airways (parenchymal/airway diseases don't cause ptosis/nasal speech).

eliminations.label: Brain stem respiratory center - Ondine curse (sleep)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: central control of automatic breathing. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: brain-stem respiratory failure impairs automatic breathing (worse in sleep) but spares voluntary breathing and would not cause ptosis/nasal speech/low FVC from muscle weakness. ✅ Correct if: central hypoventilation (Ondine curse).

eliminations.label: Pulmonary arteries - PE, no muscle weakness
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: pulmonary embolism causing dyspnea/hypoxia. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: PE doesn't cause bulbar weakness, ptosis, or a low forced vital capacity; the clinical picture is neuromuscular. ✅ Correct if: acute dyspnea with hypoxemia and V/Q mismatch.

eliminations.label: Terminal airways/alveoli - parenchymal disease
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: alveolar/interstitial disease (pulmonary fibrosis, emphysema). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: parenchymal disease can cause respiratory failure but not the non-respiratory muscle weakness (ptosis, dysphonia) seen here. ✅ Correct if: intrinsic lung disease.

eliminations.label: Upper larger airways - obstruction
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: large-airway obstruction (asthma, chronic bronchitis, laryngeal). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: airway disease doesn't explain ptosis, nasal speech, and low FVC from muscle weakness. ✅ Correct if: airflow obstruction/stridor.

reasoning: Stopping myasthenia medications precipitated a myasthenic crisis
Ptosis, nasal speech, and low forced vital capacity indicate neuromuscular (respiratory muscle) weakness
Hypercapnia (PaCO2 52) reflects hypoventilation from weak respiratory muscles
mechanism: MYASTHENIA GRAVIS (MG) is caused by AUTOANTIBODIES against postsynaptic nicotinic ACETYLCHOLINE RECEPTORS at the NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION, reducing receptor number and the muscle response to acetylcholine; weakness characteristically WORSENS WITH REPEATED use/activity. Typical features are extraocular (ptosis, diplopia), BULBAR (dysphonia/nasal speech, dysphagia, facial 'myasthenic snarl'), and proximal muscle weakness. A MYASTHENIC CRISIS is a severe exacerbation - often triggered by infection, certain drugs, or WITHDRAWAL of therapy (e.g., pyridostigmine) - in which the RESPIRATORY MUSCLES weaken, causing HYPOVENTILATION with a falling forced vital capacity and HYPERCAPNIC (and hypoxic) respiratory failure (rising PaCO2, low-normal pH). Thus the dyspnea localizes to the MUSCLES OF RESPIRATION via neuromuscular junction failure. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors treat symptoms, and crisis may require plasmapheresis/IVIG and mechanical ventilation. The distractors are central (brain-stem), vascular (pulmonary arteries), and pulmonary parenchymal/airway processes that don't cause the neuromuscular weakness seen here.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Neuro > myasthenia gravis: anti-AChR antibodies at NMJ; ptosis/diplopia, bulbar and proximal weakness worsening with use; crisis (infection/drug/withdrawal) -> respiratory muscle failure (low FVC, hypercapnia); treat AChE inhibitors, IVIG/plasmapheresis, ventilation.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: MG crisis -> respiratory muscle (NMJ) weakness -> hypoventilation/hypercapnia.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on myasthenia gravis, neuromuscular junction, bulbar weakness, forced vital capacity, or hypercapnia? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Brain-stem center = central hypoventilation; pulmonary arteries = PE; airways/alveoli = lung disease - none cause ptosis/nasal speech.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: myasthenic crisis = respiratory muscle failure (low FVC, high PaCO2); triggered by infection/drugs/med withdrawal.

firstAid.detail: Neuro: respiratory muscle (NMJ) failure -> hypercapnia, low FVC.
Pulm > central vs vascular vs parenchymal vs airway vs muscle.
Neuro > plus ventilatory support in crisis.

memoryHook: Stop the myasthenia meds and the muscles fade - including the breathing muscles; CO2 climbs and vital capacity drops: a myasthenic crisis at the neuromuscular junction.
